notes.b: Food packaging is made from six main materials, and each one suits certain foods because of its properties. Knowing a material's strengths tells you what it is used for.
points: Metals (aluminium and tin) are strong, airtight and can be heat-processed, so they are used for canned fish and fruit, takeaway containers and aerosol whipped cream. Tins are lacquered inside so the metal does not react with the food.

Glass (jars and bottles) is hygienic, transparent, impervious, resealable and reusable, so it is used for beverages, mayonnaise, sauces, preserves and cooking oil. Its drawbacks are that it is heavy and breakable.

Plastics (polythene, PET and similar polymers) are lightweight, flexible, moisture-proof, transparent and can be heat-sealed. They are used for polythene bags, PET soft drink bottles, yoghurt pots, dairy spreads and dried pasta, but are mostly non-biodegradable.
Polystyrene is lightweight, insulating, shock-absorbing, easily moulded and stackable, which suits egg trays and takeaway trays and containers. It is not readily biodegradable.

Paper and cardboard are light, inexpensive, easy to print on and renewable. They are used for cereal boxes, egg cartons and paper bags for bread, cakes, flour and sugar, but they are not moisture-proof unless coated.
Waxed cartons use a wax coating to make the board waterproof, so they are cheap, lightweight, printable and heat-sealable. They are recyclable or biodegradable according to the scheme.
notes.tip: Paper packaging is not moisture-proof; it only resists moisture when waxed or coated, so don't call it moisture-proof. When asked for the benefit of polystyrene, a glass bottle or a waxed carton, give a different property for each.

notes.b: A pack has to do a job for the food inside it, so examiners expect you to list the qualities a good pack needs. Which qualities matter most depends on the food.
points: Packaging must be strong and durable enough to survive handling and transport, so the food arrives undamaged.
It must be airtight or moisture- and vapour-proof, depending on the food, so the food does not dry out, go soft or spoil.
It must be hygienic and safe, and must not react with or taint the food, so it should be odourless.
It should be easy to open and, where needed, easy to reseal, so the consumer can use it a little at a time.
It should be lightweight, stackable and easy to store, which makes it cheaper to transport and easier to shelve.
It should be heat resistant where the food is heated in the pack, and printable so that labels can be applied.
It should be attractive to the consumer and economical to produce.
notes.tip: When asked for desirable qualities of packaging, give specific ones from this list, such as strong, airtight, hygienic or printable, rather than vague words like 'good'.

notes.b: Packaging does more than wrap food. It has four jobs that examiners ask for, and a fifth, convenience, is also credited.
points: Protection: packaging guards food against physical damage and against contamination by micro-organisms and dirt, so the food stays safe and intact.
Containment: it holds the product in the portion size intended for the consumer.
Information: it carries the product name, ingredients, nutrition and storage details, as well as weight, allergens, cooking instructions and branding.
Tamper evidence: a sealed pack shows whether the contents have been interfered with, so the consumer can tell if it has been opened.
Convenience: packs that are easy to open, reseal, store and carry make the food easier to use.
notes.tip: For a question on the role of packaging, write about suitability for purpose, environmental impact and information, with a material-by-material comparison. Name recycling and Re-turn, and list what a label contains.

notes.b: Packaging that protects food can also create waste. How much harm it does depends on whether the material is renewable, biodegradable (breaks down naturally) and recyclable (reprocessed into new products).
points: Metal and plastic packaging is not biodegradable and is made from non-renewable resources, but both can be recycled.
Glass can be reused and recycled indefinitely without losing quality.
Paper and cardboard are made from a renewable resource, are biodegradable and are widely recyclable.
Polystyrene is bulky and not readily biodegradable, so its environmental impact depends on whether it is collected for recycling.
The impact is reduced by using less packaging, reusing containers and recycling materials.

In Ireland, the Re-turn deposit return scheme supports recycling of plastic drinks bottles and aluminium and steel cans by refunding a deposit: 15c for containers under 500 ml and 25c for 500 ml and over.

The scheme launched nationwide on 1 February 2026 for PET plastic bottles and aluminium or steel cans from 150 ml to 3 litres, under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations 2021 (S.I. 599 of 2021).
notes.tip: The statement that all packaging is biodegradable and recyclable is false. Biodegradable and recyclable are different: glass is recyclable but not biodegradable, while paper is both. Name Re-turn when asked about the environment in an Irish context.

notes.b: Two kinds of packaging answer particular problems: one makes food last longer, the other makes the pack itself break down after use.
points: Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP): the air is removed and replaced with a controlled mixture of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen, and the pack is heat sealed.
The gas mixture slows the growth of bacteria, yeasts and moulds, so the shelf life of the food is extended. It also helps keep the food's colour.
MAP is used for fresh meat, fish, fruit and vegetables, baked goods and cheese.
Biodegradable packaging breaks down into the raw materials of nature, with micro-organisms doing much of the work.
Examples of biodegradable packaging: paper bags for bread, cakes, sugar and flour, and cardboard for cereals, takeaway foods and eggs.
Diagram: a labelled sealed pack showing the gas mixture inside the tray and the heat-sealed film lid.
notes.tip: When explaining MAP, give the gas mixture and say it slows micro-organisms, then name a food it is used for. MAP is a packaging technique, not an additive or preservative added to the food. For biodegradable, say it breaks down into the raw materials of nature and give paper bags or cardboard as examples.

notes.b: Irish food labels follow Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, and the FSAI coordinates enforcement.
points: The European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014 (S.I. No. 556 of 2014, in force 13 December 2014) give effect in Ireland to Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, and official agencies working under FSAI service contracts carry out enforcement.
The name of the food must be stated, along with a list of ingredients in descending order by weight, so the main ingredient comes first.

Allergens such as milk, egg, nuts and gluten cereals must be emphasised within the ingredients list, so people with allergies can spot them. The Regulation lists 14 allergens, including cereals containing gluten, milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish, crustaceans, molluscs, soya, celery, mustard, sesame, lupin, sulphur dioxide and sulphites.
The net quantity must be stated, and the name and address of the food business operator must appear on the label.

A use-by date is given for highly perishable food and is a food safety date, so do not eat after it. A best-before date (the date of minimum durability) is a quality date, after which the food may still be safe.
Storage conditions and cooking or usage instructions must be given, for example keep refrigerated or stir before use.
The country of origin or place of provenance is given where the law requires it.
Additives are identified by their class name followed by the specific name or E number, for example preservative: E202.
Labels also carry a lot or batch code, which lets a product be traced and recalled if there is a problem.
notes.tip: Don't swap the two dates: use-by is for safety and best-before is for quality. Don't say food becomes unsafe the day after its best-before date.

notes.b: The nutrition declaration is a standard table that lets shoppers compare foods on the same terms. Claims on the front of a pack are separate, and need careful reading.
points: The mandatory nutrition declaration gives seven items: energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt.
Values are given per 100 g or 100 ml, which allows fair comparison between products, and often per portion as well.
Claims such as low fat, high in fibre or contains live cultures must be accurate and not misleading, and nutrition and health claims must meet the EU rules, set by Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
Low fat does not necessarily mean low sugar, salt or energy, so the full declaration must be read.
notes.tip: In a question on choosing convenience foods, compare the nutrition declaration per 100 g and make the point that claims do not tell the whole story, so the full label must be read. Front-of-pack traffic-light labelling is voluntary in Ireland, so don't state it as a legal requirement.

notes.h: Labelling as a source of consumer information
notes.b: A label is the consumer's main source of information at the point of purchase. It helps shoppers choose, stay safe and avoid waste.
points: Labels allow consumers to compare products on energy, fat, sugar and salt, rather than being guided by brand, pictures or health claims.
Consumers following a low-salt, low-saturated-fat or high-fibre diet can select products by their declared values.
Ingredients and allergen emphasis protect people with coeliac disease, milk, egg, nut or other allergies.
Use-by and best-before dates, storage and reheating instructions protect safety and reduce food waste.
The origin on the label lets consumers choose to buy Irish.
The manufacturer's details and the lot code support traceability and complaints.
Quality assurance (such as the Bord Bia mark), organic, fair-trade and gluten-free marks guide consumers with particular ethical or dietary choices.
notes.tip: Questions ask for three benefits of labelling or four items of consumer information with the importance of each. Pick distinct points such as comparing products, special diets, safety and waste, and traceability, and say why each matters. In a food profile, list the label contents: name, ingredients, nutrition, date, storage and manufacturer.

keyTerms.definition: Packaging in which the air is replaced with a controlled mixture of gases, then heat sealed, to slow the spoilage of food.
Packaging that breaks down into the raw materials of nature through the action of micro-organisms.
Describes a material that can be collected and reprocessed into new products.
A coating applied inside metal cans so that the metal does not react with the food.
A sealed pack design that shows clearly whether the contents have been opened or interfered with.
A date after which a highly perishable food should not be eaten, for safety reasons.
A date after which a food may lose quality, though it is not necessarily unsafe.
Showing an allergenic ingredient in the ingredients list in a way that makes it stand out, such as bold type.
The standard panel of energy and nutrient values that manufacturers must give on the label of most pre-packed foods.
A batch code printed on packaging that allows a product to be traced back through production and distribution.

factCards.term: Five desirable characteristics of food packaging
factCards.definition: Strong and durable; airtight or moisture-proof; hygienic and safe; easy to open and reseal; lightweight and easy to store.

factCards.term: Three advantages of paper and cardboard packaging
factCards.definition: They are light and relatively inexpensive, easy to print on for labelling, and made from a renewable resource that is biodegradable and recyclable.

factCards.term: Gases used in modified atmosphere packaging
factCards.definition: Carbon dioxide, nitrogen and oxygen, in a controlled mixture.

factCards.term: Why nitrogen is used in food packs
factCards.definition: It is inert, so it displaces oxygen and prevents oxidation and spoilage.

factCards.term: Items in the mandatory nutrition declaration
factCards.definition: Energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt.

factCards.term: Difference between use-by and best-before dates
factCards.definition: A use-by date is a food safety date for highly perishable food; a best-before date is a quality date.
Comparing products, selecting diets, protecting people with allergies, and reducing waste through correct storage and use.

factCards.term: Purpose of lacquer in a tin can
factCards.definition: It stops the metal reacting with the food.

questions.prompt: Explain why glass and paper are used to package different types of food. Give one example of each material and a reason it suits the food it holds.
questions.model: Glass is used for beverages, sauces, preserves and oil. It is transparent so the product can be seen, it is inert so it does not react with the food, and it is hygienic and reusable or recyclable. Paper and cardboard are used for cereals, eggs, bread and cakes. They are light, cheap, easy to print on for labelling and protective enough for dry or fragile foods, and they are biodegradable and recyclable. Full marks need one example and one reason for each material.

questions.prompt: Assess how the packaging and labelling of a food product serve the manufacturer, the consumer and the environment, and identify one limitation of each.
questions.model: Manufacturer: packaging protects the product, extends its shelf life through methods such as modified atmosphere packaging, carries branding and gives a tamper-evident seal; the label meets legal requirements and identifies the batch for traceability. Limitation: packaging adds cost and must meet the labelling rules, which can be time-consuming. Consumer: the label gives the ingredients in order of weight, allergens emphasised, the nutrition declaration per 100 g and per portion, use-by or best-before dates and storage instructions, so choices and safety are informed. Limitation: a label can be misread, as low fat does not mean low sugar, salt or energy. Environment: material choice matters; glass is reusable and recyclable, paper and cardboard are renewable and biodegradable, and metal and plastic are recyclable but not biodegradable. Limitation: excess packaging creates waste, so reducing and reusing it is the best response.
